lessons.misconception: Bernoulli and Poiseuille describe different idealizations; do not mix their assumptions blindly.

workedExample.prompt: A tube’s radius doubles while pressure difference, viscosity, and length stay fixed. Predict ideal laminar flow rate.
steps: Use Q proportional to r⁴.
The new-to-old radius ratio is two.
The flow ratio is 2⁴ = 16.

check.prompt: An incompressible fluid enters a region with half the cross-sectional area at steady flow. Speed becomes:
check.explanation: Continuity requires A1v1 = A2v2, so halving area doubles speed.

transfer.prompt: At fixed radius and other conditions, doubling viscosity in Poiseuille’s model changes flow to:
transfer.explanation: Flow is inversely proportional to viscosity, so doubling viscosity halves flow.

visual.caption: Flow rate and local speed are different quantities connected by area.

lessons.subject: physics
lessons.title: Electric fields, potential, and capacitance
lessons.summary: Electric field is force per unit positive test charge. Electric potential is potential energy per unit charge, so ΔU = qΔV. A charge’s force direction depends on its sign. Capacitors store separated charge with Q = CV and energy ½CV². In a parallel-plate model, larger plate area increases capacitance and larger separation decreases it, assuming the same dielectric.
keyPoints: F = qE; negative charges accelerate opposite the field direction.
Q = CV relates stored charge, capacitance, and voltage.
lessons.misconception: Electric potential is a scalar; electric field is a vector.

workedExample.prompt: A 2 μC positive charge moves through a +3 V potential difference. Find its potential-energy change.
steps: Use ΔU = qΔV.
Convert charge to 2 × 10⁻⁶ C.
Multiply by +3 V.

check.prompt: An electron in an electric field experiences force:
check.explanation: The electron’s negative charge reverses the direction in F = qE.

transfer.prompt: A 4 μF capacitor at 5 V stores what charge?
transfer.explanation: Q = CV = 4 μF × 5 V = 20 μC.

visual.caption: Choose force reasoning for fields and energy reasoning for potential differences.

lessons.subject: physics
lessons.title: Circuits and electrical power
lessons.summary: Ohm’s law V = IR applies to an ohmic component under its stated conditions. Series resistors carry the same current and their resistances add. Parallel branches share the same voltage, and their conductances add. Electrical power can be written P = IV, I²R, or V²/R for a resistor. Identify whether voltage or current is fixed before predicting how a resistance change affects power.
keyPoints: Series: Req = R1 + R2 + …
Parallel: 1/Req = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + …
lessons.misconception: Increasing resistance does not always increase power; the fixed variable matters.

workedExample.prompt: Two 6 Ω resistors are in parallel across 12 V. Find total current.
steps: Two equal parallel resistors give Req = 3 Ω.
Use I = V/Req.

check.prompt: Two resistors of 2 Ω and 4 Ω in series have equivalent resistance:
check.explanation: Series resistances add: 2 + 4 = 6 Ω.

transfer.prompt: At fixed voltage, doubling a resistor’s resistance changes its power to:
transfer.explanation: P = V²/R, so doubling R at fixed V halves power.

visual.caption: State the fixed source condition before using a power formula.

lessons.subject: physics
lessons.title: Waves, sound, and frequency
lessons.summary: Wave speed, wavelength, and frequency satisfy v = fλ. Frequency is set by the source; when a wave enters a different medium, its speed and wavelength may change while frequency remains continuous across the boundary. Sound intensity is power per area. The decibel scale uses 10 log10(I/I0), so a tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB and a hundredfold increase adds 20 dB.
keyPoints: v = fλ.
A 10 dB increase corresponds to tenfold intensity, not tenfold perceived loudness.
lessons.misconception: Frequency and amplitude are separate properties.

workedExample.prompt: A sound wave travels at 340 m/s with frequency 170 Hz. Find wavelength.
steps: Rearrange v = fλ to λ = v/f.
Divide 340 by 170.
The units m/s divided by 1/s give meters.

check.prompt: At constant wave speed, doubling frequency changes wavelength to:
check.explanation: Wavelength is inversely proportional to frequency when speed is fixed.

transfer.prompt: Intensity increases by a factor of 100. The sound level rises by:

visual.caption: Separate timing, spacing, and amplitude when describing a wave.

lessons.subject: physics
lessons.title: Light, lenses, and image formation
lessons.summary: Geometric optics tracks rays through reflection and refraction. Snell’s law relates refractive index to ray angle measured from the normal. A thin lens follows 1/f = 1/do + 1/di with a consistent sign convention. For a converging lens and an object beyond the focal point, a real image can form on the opposite side. Magnification gives image size and orientation.
keyPoints: Measure refraction angles from the normal.
Lens power in diopters is 1/f when f is in meters.
lessons.misconception: A converging lens does not always produce a real image; object position matters.

workedExample.prompt: A converging lens has f = 10 cm and an object at 20 cm. Find image distance.
steps: Subtract 1/20 from both sides.
1/di = 1/20, so di = 20 cm.
workedExample.answer: 20 cm on the image side under the usual real-is-positive convention.

check.prompt: A converging lens with focal length +0.5 m has power:
check.explanation: Power is 1/0.5 = +2 diopters.

transfer.prompt: Light enters a higher-index medium at a nonzero angle. It generally bends:
choices: Exactly parallel to the boundary always
Without any change in direction always
transfer.explanation: Snell’s law gives a smaller angle from the normal in the higher-index medium.

visual.caption: Use a ray sketch to check the sign and plausibility of the calculated image.

lessons.subject: physics
lessons.title: Radioactive decay and quantitative data
lessons.summary: Radioactive decay is probabilistic for individual nuclei but predictable for a large sample. After each half-life, half the remaining undecayed nuclei remain, so N = N0(1/2)^(t/t½). Distinguish physical decay from biological elimination when reading a tracer experiment. More broadly, quantitative passages require careful axes, units, control comparisons, and uncertainty; a trend can be real without identifying its cause.
keyPoints: After n half-lives, the remaining fraction is (1/2)^n.
Activity is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei for a fixed isotope.
lessons.misconception: Half-life is not the time for every nucleus to decay.

workedExample.prompt: A sample begins with 80 units of activity and has a 3-hour half-life. Find activity after 9 hours, ignoring biological elimination.
steps: Nine hours contains three half-lives.
Halve the activity three times: 80 → 40 → 20 → 10.
Keep the physical-decay assumption explicit.

check.prompt: After two half-lives, what fraction of the original undecayed nuclei remains?
check.explanation: Two successive halvings leave one fourth.

transfer.prompt: A graph plots concentration in μM, but an equation requires M. A value of 5 μM is:
transfer.explanation: The prefix micro means 10⁻⁶, so 5 μM = 5 × 10⁻⁶ M.

visual.caption: Read the experimental assumptions before applying an ideal decay model.

lessons.subject: cars
lessons.title: Finding the main claim
lessons.summary: A useful main-idea statement explains what the author wants the reader to accept, not merely the topic under discussion. Track the problem introduced, the qualification added, and the resolution proposed. Test a candidate summary against the whole passage: a claim that fits one vivid example but misses the conclusion is too narrow. The short original passages here isolate one skill before full-length practice.
keyPoints: Separate the topic from the author’s position.
Keep the author’s qualifications in your summary.
lessons.misconception: The most memorable detail is not necessarily the main point.

workedExample.prompt: In the museum passage, how do replicas contribute to the author’s overall proposal?
steps: The opening identifies a cost of viewing artifacts only as protected shapes.
The author preserves the need to protect fragile originals.
Replicas allow participation without sacrificing conservation.

check.prompt: Which statement best expresses the main claim?
choices: Museums should let visitors handle every original object.
Preservation and participation can be combined through different treatment of originals and replicas.
Replicas are more historically valuable than originals.
Cooking vessels are the only artifacts worth displaying.
check.explanation: The conclusion reconciles preservation with participation. The other choices remove qualifications or overfocus on an example.
check.passage: A museum that places every object behind glass may protect its collection while obscuring why the objects mattered. A cooking vessel was once lifted, heated, and passed between people; viewed only as a shape, it loses part of its history. Yet unrestricted handling would destroy fragile artifacts. The solution is not to abandon preservation, but to supplement protected originals with replicas that visitors can use. Conservation and participation need not be rivals when each is assigned an appropriate object.

transfer.prompt: Which statement best captures the argument?
choices: Book ownership alone defines library quality.
Collections and support for using them jointly make libraries useful.
Libraries should replace all books with staff.
Catalogues are more valuable than every book.
transfer.explanation: The passage argues for both resources and navigation, explicitly rejecting either as sufficient alone.
transfer.passage: A public library is often praised for the number of books it owns. Ownership, however, is a poor measure if readers cannot locate or interpret what they need. Staff guidance, accessible catalogues, and welcoming spaces turn possession into use. This does not make collections irrelevant: an excellent guide cannot retrieve a book the library lacks. A useful library therefore joins a strong collection to the means of navigating it.

visual.caption: Summarize the relationship among ideas, not just the subject matter.

lessons.passage: A museum that places every object behind glass may protect its collection while obscuring why the objects mattered. A cooking vessel was once lifted, heated, and passed between people; viewed only as a shape, it loses part of its history. Yet unrestricted handling would destroy fragile artifacts. The solution is not to abandon preservation, but to supplement protected originals with replicas that visitors can use. Conservation and participation need not be rivals when each is assigned an appropriate object.

lessons.subject: cars
lessons.title: Tone and qualified judgments
lessons.summary: Tone questions ask for the author’s attitude, which often combines approval with a specific reservation. Underline evaluative words, then identify what each evaluates. A passage can praise a result while criticizing a larger claim about it. Prefer a tone description proportionate to the language: measured criticism is different from contempt, and qualified support is different from wholehearted celebration.
keyPoints: Tie tone labels to evaluative language.
Identify the object of praise or criticism.
lessons.misconception: A single negative word does not make the whole passage hostile.

workedExample.prompt: What does “admirably readable” do in the translation passage?
steps: It explicitly praises one feature: readability.
Later sentences identify a separate loss: strangeness.
Together they create a qualified evaluation, not total rejection.
workedExample.answer: It establishes genuine but limited praise.

check.prompt: The author’s attitude toward the translation is best described as:
check.explanation: The author values accessibility while criticizing loss of the original’s unsettling quality.
check.passage: The new translation is admirably readable. Its sentences move with an ease that earlier versions rarely achieved, and readers once deterred by the work may now enter it. Still, the translator’s preference for familiar idioms sometimes erases the original’s productive strangeness. A voice that should unsettle us occasionally sounds like a friendly columnist. Accessibility is an achievement, but it is not the only achievement a translation should seek.

transfer.prompt: The author is most critical of:
choices: Claims that the bridge alone solves broader social problems
transfer.explanation: The passage praises the bridge but rejects exaggerated claims about what it can accomplish.
transfer.passage: The city’s new pedestrian bridge is graceful and offers a convenient crossing. Officials also call it a cure for the neighborhood’s isolation. That claim asks a bridge to do the work of affordable transit, reliable services, and economic opportunity. The structure deserves appreciation for what it supplies, not a mythology that excuses the absence of everything else.

visual.caption: Attach attitude to a specific object or claim.

lessons.passage: The new translation is admirably readable. Its sentences move with an ease that earlier versions rarely achieved, and readers once deterred by the work may now enter it. Still, the translator’s preference for familiar idioms sometimes erases the original’s productive strangeness. A voice that should unsettle us occasionally sounds like a friendly columnist. Accessibility is an achievement, but it is not the only achievement a translation should seek.

lessons.subject: cars
lessons.title: Making supported inferences
lessons.summary: An inference connects passage evidence to a conclusion the author need not state word for word. Keep the inferential step small. Ask what must be true, or is strongly supported, if the author’s reasoning is accepted. Avoid importing an attractive outside explanation. A good inference preserves scope: criticism of one policy feature does not establish that the entire institution is harmful.
keyPoints: Use the smallest justified step beyond the text.
Preserve words such as some, may, and often.
lessons.misconception: A possibility consistent with the passage is not automatically a supported inference.

workedExample.prompt: What distinction drives the plaza argument?
steps: The plaza permits many uses in principle.
Its physical features may discourage actual use.
Therefore permission and practical invitation are different.
workedExample.answer: A design can allow an activity without encouraging it.

check.prompt: The author would most likely agree that:
choices: All plazas should prohibit large events.
A legally open space can still discourage gathering.
Shade is the only meaningful design feature.
Flexibility always makes a place successful.
check.explanation: The passage distinguishes technical permission from conditions that make people comfortable participating.
check.passage: An architect may describe an empty plaza as flexible because it accommodates many possible events. But possibility is not the same as invitation. A place without shade, seating, or clear entrances may technically permit gathering while discouraging anyone from beginning it. Design should be judged not only by the activities it fails to prohibit, but also by the activities it makes comfortable to attempt.

transfer.prompt: Which inference is best supported?
choices: Students unfamiliar with school procedures may face greater barriers to proposing projects.
Independent projects are always inferior to classes.
transfer.explanation: The rules favor institutional familiarity, so less familiar students may face greater barriers. The stronger alternatives are unsupported.
transfer.passage: A school advertises that students may propose independent projects. Yet proposals require a detailed budget, a faculty sponsor, and approval during a single week in September. These rules may have administrative purposes, but they also favor students who already know how the institution works. Formal permission does not by itself ensure that an opportunity is practically available.

visual.caption: An inference should need the passage, not an outside story.

lessons.passage: An architect may describe an empty plaza as flexible because it accommodates many possible events. But possibility is not the same as invitation. A place without shade, seating, or clear entrances may technically permit gathering while discouraging anyone from beginning it. Design should be judged not only by the activities it fails to prohibit, but also by the activities it makes comfortable to attempt.

lessons.subject: cars
lessons.title: The function of examples
lessons.summary: A function question asks why a detail appears in the argument. Distinguish the example’s literal content from the claim it supports. Try replacing the example with a blank labeled “evidence for ___.” If the label captures the surrounding reasoning, you have identified its role. Examples may illustrate, qualify, contrast, or challenge; they do not always prove a universal rule.
keyPoints: Ask what claim an example helps establish.
Read the sentences before and after the detail.
lessons.misconception: Explaining what an example describes is not the same as explaining its argumentative function.

workedExample.prompt: Why does the historian mention sleep interrupted by street noise?
steps: The detail represents an ordinary lived experience.
Official categories may omit that kind of experience.
It illustrates how diaries expand the archive’s coverage.
workedExample.answer: To show a kind of experience that official reports may miss.

check.prompt: The shop-closing example primarily serves to:
choices: Prove that all official reports are false.
Argue that commerce alone defines city life.
Show that diaries should replace every other source.
Illustrate experiences diaries may preserve beyond administrative categories.
check.explanation: It supports the broader value of diaries while the final sentence explicitly rejects replacing the archive.
check.passage: A historian argues that diaries deserve a larger role in accounts of city life. Official reports record what administrators counted, but a diary may reveal the interruption of sleep by street noise or the meaning of a familiar shop closing. Such details are not merely decoration. They disclose forms of experience that an administrative category may never have been designed to capture. Diaries remain selective and imperfect; their value lies in expanding, not replacing, the archive.

transfer.prompt: The contrast between dishes and seating arrangement helps the critic show:
choices: That the novel contains no social argument.
That food descriptions are accidental decoration.
Economic change alongside persistent social hierarchy.
transfer.explanation: Changing dishes register income change; fixed seats represent a stable hierarchy.
transfer.passage: A critic says a novel’s repeated descriptions of meals are central to its argument. The dishes change as the family’s income changes, but the seating arrangement remains fixed. Food registers economic movement while the table preserves social hierarchy. The meals therefore let readers see two kinds of change at once: one occurring and one resisted.

visual.caption: Replace the detail with its job in the argument.

lessons.passage: A historian argues that diaries deserve a larger role in accounts of city life. Official reports record what administrators counted, but a diary may reveal the interruption of sleep by street noise or the meaning of a familiar shop closing. Such details are not merely decoration. They disclose forms of experience that an administrative category may never have been designed to capture. Diaries remain selective and imperfect; their value lies in expanding, not replacing, the archive.

lessons.subject: cars
lessons.title: Assumptions and missing links
lessons.summary: An assumption is an unstated bridge needed for a conclusion to follow from its reasons. Identify the evidence, state the conclusion, and ask what connects them. A useful test is to negate a proposed assumption: if the argument collapses or is seriously weakened, the assumption may be necessary. Do not confuse something that would make the conclusion nicer with something the reasoning requires.
keyPoints: Map evidence → missing bridge → conclusion.
Use negation to test a proposed necessary assumption.
lessons.misconception: An assumption need not be a fact the author explicitly states.

workedExample.prompt: What practical assumption supports the garden-hours proposal?
steps: The reason is that residents are unavailable before closing.
The proposed remedy is later opening.
The remedy assumes some residents would use the garden during later hours.
workedExample.answer: At least some residents would visit if later access were offered.

check.prompt: Which assumption most directly supports the proposal?
choices: Every resident prefers gardens to all other activities.
The garden should remain open all night.
Some residents unable to visit now would be able to visit during extended hours.
check.explanation: The proposal requires later access to address a real availability barrier; universal preferences and all-night opening are unnecessary.
check.passage: The town should extend evening hours at its public garden, a council member argues, because many residents finish work after the gates close. The garden already has paths and lighting suitable for later visits. If access is to serve residents rather than merely satisfy a posted schedule, the hours should overlap with the time residents can actually come.

transfer.prompt: Which assumption is most important to the university’s claim of equal understanding?
choices: Interaction in the seminar adds no indispensable learning beyond the recorded instructor material.
Recordings contain fewer facts than live lectures.
transfer.explanation: The proposal equates content delivery with understanding, which requires the omitted interactive elements not to be essential.
transfer.passage: A university plans to replace a required seminar with recorded lectures, arguing that students will gain the same understanding while enjoying greater scheduling freedom. The proposal emphasizes that the recordings contain all the material presented by the instructor. It says little about the questions students previously asked or the arguments they developed with one another.

visual.caption: Find what must connect the premise to the recommendation.

lessons.passage: The town should extend evening hours at its public garden, a council member argues, because many residents finish work after the gates close. The garden already has paths and lighting suitable for later visits. If access is to serve residents rather than merely satisfy a posted schedule, the hours should overlap with the time residents can actually come.

lessons.subject: cars
lessons.title: Strengthening and weakening an argument
lessons.summary: New evidence strengthens an argument when it makes the move from premises to conclusion more credible; it weakens when it exposes a competing explanation or undermines a necessary link. Focus on the actual conclusion rather than a nearby topic. For causal claims, ask whether another change could explain the outcome. A weakening fact need not prove the conclusion false; reducing support is enough.
keyPoints: Target the link between evidence and conclusion.
A competing cause can weaken a causal inference.
lessons.misconception: A fact can weaken an argument without disproving its conclusion completely.

workedExample.prompt: Why does the reopened rail station matter to the public-art claim?
steps: The conclusion assigns the traffic increase to art.
The station reopened at the same time and could bring visitors.
It supplies an alternative cause not separated by the report.

check.prompt: Which finding would most strengthen the planner’s causal claim?
choices: Most additional visitors report coming specifically to see the art, and comparable station reopenings without art did not raise weekend visits.
The station has a long name.
check.explanation: The finding links visits to art and addresses the obvious transit alternative; the other facts do not test the causal link.
check.passage: After a neighborhood installed public art, weekend foot traffic rose. A planner concludes that the art attracted the additional visitors and recommends the same strategy elsewhere. During the same month, a nearby rail station also reopened after a long closure. The planner’s report counts visitors but does not ask why they came.

transfer.prompt: Which follow-up would best address the main weakness?
choices: Compare randomly assigned readers with the same prior preparation, varying only the introduction.
Use a more decorative introduction font without controlling groups.
Ask the editor whether introductions are valuable.
Measure the length of the essays only.
transfer.explanation: Balancing prior preparation while varying the introduction helps isolate its effect on comprehension.
transfer.passage: An editor argues that adding short introductions to difficult essays improves readers’ understanding. Readers who received introductions performed better on a comprehension test than readers who did not. However, the two groups came from different classes, and the introduction group had already studied the essay’s historical setting.

visual.caption: Ask whether the added fact changes support for the specific conclusion.

lessons.passage: After a neighborhood installed public art, weekend foot traffic rose. A planner concludes that the art attracted the additional visitors and recommends the same strategy elsewhere. During the same month, a nearby rail station also reopened after a long closure. The planner’s report counts visitors but does not ask why they came.

lessons.title: Applying a principle to a new case
lessons.summary: Application questions move an argument into a new setting. First express the passage’s principle without its surface details. Then choose a new case with the same relationship among goals, methods, and constraints. Matching vocabulary is weak evidence; matching logical structure is strong evidence. Keep qualifications intact so a limited principle does not become an unlimited permission.
keyPoints: Abstract the principle before comparing options.
Match relationships, not shared nouns.
lessons.misconception: An analogy about the same subject can still have the wrong logical structure.

workedExample.prompt: State the theatre passage’s principle without mentioning theatre.
steps: The intended effect is the goal.
Changed conditions can make old methods ineffective.
Changing the method can preserve the goal.
workedExample.answer: Adapt methods to preserve an intended effect under new conditions.

check.prompt: Which case best applies the author’s principle?
choices: A museum discards every object because it is old.
A musician changes an arrangement so a new instrument can preserve the original melody’s expressive effect.
A reader refuses to read any translation.
An athlete ignores the rules to guarantee victory.
check.explanation: The musician adapts means to changed conditions while preserving the intended effect, matching the argument.
check.passage: A community theatre preserves a play’s historical setting but changes its staging to suit a small outdoor courtyard. Purists object that any departure from the first production is a betrayal. Yet a production that mechanically copies old stage directions may fail to reproduce their effect in a new space. Fidelity can require changing the means when the conditions of performance change.

transfer.prompt: Which example best fits the map passage’s principle?
choices: A transit diagram simplifies geographic distances to make transfers easier to understand.
A map removes the only bridge needed for the route.
A manual hides essential safety steps to look shorter.
A schedule lists random departure times.
transfer.explanation: The transit diagram omits task-irrelevant precision to improve navigation; the other cases remove essential information or become inaccurate for the task.
transfer.passage: A teacher uses a handwritten map rather than a satellite image to explain a walking route. The map omits roofs, parked cars, and most side streets while enlarging the important turns. Its distortions are deliberate. A representation can be less complete yet more useful for a particular task, provided the omitted details are irrelevant to that task.

lessons.subject: cars
lessons.title: Mapping argument structure
lessons.summary: A passage map records what each part does: introduce a dispute, offer evidence, qualify a claim, answer an objection, or propose a resolution. This is more useful than collecting isolated facts. Transition words often signal changes in direction, but the relationships between sentences matter more than the words alone. A final qualification may narrow an earlier claim without reversing it.
keyPoints: Label paragraph jobs in a few words.
Track whether a later point supports, limits, or rejects an earlier one.
lessons.misconception: A qualification is not necessarily a contradiction.

workedExample.prompt: How does the archive passage move from its opening to its conclusion?
steps: It presents two extreme positions.
It identifies distinct strengths of digital and physical forms.
It recommends choosing based on the research question.
workedExample.answer: Opposing extremes → complementary strengths → task-based choice.

check.prompt: The author’s response to the two opening positions is to:
choices: Accept the first and ignore the second.
Reject the forced choice by distinguishing the questions each form can answer.
Deny that physical objects contain information.
check.explanation: The passage replaces an either-or dispute with a question-dependent comparison.
check.passage: Some critics call digital archives a replacement for physical libraries. Others dismiss them as pale imitations. Both positions miss the more useful comparison. Digital access can make a rare document available across great distances, while the physical object may reveal paper, binding, or marks lost in a scan. The two forms answer overlapping but nonidentical questions. A research practice that understands this difference will ask which form a question requires.

transfer.prompt: The discussion of delivery workers primarily:
choices: Proves the quiet streets do not exist.
Shows the author opposes every restriction.
Introduces an unrelated topic with no argumentative role.
Qualifies support for the restrictions by identifying an accommodation need.
transfer.explanation: The author maintains support but adds a condition for a fairer implementation.
transfer.passage: The essay first describes a city’s unusually quiet streets. It then reveals that cars are restricted during certain hours, before considering the delivery workers who must reorganize their routes. The author ends by defending the restrictions while urging better accommodations for those workers. The quiet opening is thus neither a complete account nor a false one; it is the first layer of an evaluation.

visual.caption: Make a map of reasoning moves rather than a list of facts.

lessons.subject: cars
lessons.title: Words in context and figurative language
lessons.summary: A word’s relevant meaning is the one supported by its role in the sentence and argument. When an author uses a term figuratively, translate the relationship rather than choosing the most literal dictionary sense. Substitute a plain-language paraphrase and reread the sentence. If the paraphrase preserves the argument while avoiding unsupported implications, it is a strong interpretation.
keyPoints: Use surrounding claims to constrain meaning.
Translate a metaphor into the relationship it expresses.
lessons.misconception: A familiar word can carry a specialized or figurative meaning in context.

workedExample.prompt: What does “archive” mean when applied to repeated city practices?
steps: The practices carry traces of the past.
They also select and reshape those traces.
The term highlights their role as historical evidence, not a physical storage room.
workedExample.answer: A source through which aspects of the past are preserved and interpreted.

check.prompt: In context, calling practices an “archive” primarily emphasizes their:
choices: Ability to supply evidence about the past
Exact duplication of every past event
check.explanation: The author treats practices as selective historical evidence and explicitly denies unchanged preservation.
check.passage: A city’s memory is not stored only in monuments. It also resides in repeated practices: a market held on the same corner, an annual procession, a customary route to school. Calling these practices an archive does not mean that they preserve the past unchanged. Like written records, they select, omit, and reorganize. Their fragility is therefore not a reason to exclude them from historical attention, but a reason to observe them carefully.

transfer.prompt: The phrase “material of music” most nearly means that silence:
choices: Is a physical substance heavier than sound
Is an element used to organize musical meaning
transfer.explanation: The following sentences explain the functional role of pauses in shaping expectation and relationships.
transfer.passage: The composer calls silence a material of music. She does not suggest that silence is a substance that can be weighed. Rather, pauses shape expectation, separate phrases, and alter the meaning of the sounds around them. A score that records only notes would fail to specify the relationships that make those notes intelligible.

visual.caption: Test meanings in the actual sentence rather than in isolation.

lessons.subject: cars
lessons.title: Scope, certainty, and answer traps
lessons.summary: An answer can sound relevant while making a stronger claim than the passage permits. Compare quantifiers, causal language, and certainty: some is not all, may is not must, and association is not proof of cause. Also watch for reversed relationships and claims that are true in the world but unsupported in the passage. Evidence-based elimination means naming the specific mismatch, not simply calling an answer too extreme.
keyPoints: Match the author’s degree of certainty.
Distinguish observation from universal or causal claims.
lessons.misconception: A cautious conclusion is not the same as saying the evidence has no value.

workedExample.prompt: Why does the history-lecture author stop short of a causal promise?
steps: The survey finds an association.
Either direction of influence could explain it.
The design does not distinguish those directions.
workedExample.answer: The evidence supports a connection but not a settled causal direction.

check.prompt: Which conclusion stays within the passage’s scope?
choices: Neighborhood attachment always prevents lecture attendance.
Attendance and attachment are associated, but causal direction remains unresolved.
The survey contains no potentially useful information.
check.explanation: This preserves both the observed association and the author’s causal caution.
check.passage: A survey found that residents who attend local history lectures report greater attachment to their neighborhood. This association is worth exploring. It may be that the lectures deepen attachment, or that already attached residents are more likely to attend. The survey cannot distinguish these possibilities. It supports further inquiry into the connection, not a confident promise that lectures will create belonging wherever they are offered.

transfer.prompt: Which claim exceeds the report’s stated support?
choices: Every wetland restoration will increase bird diversity in every climate.
The observed projects showed an encouraging pattern.
Rainfall could be relevant to interpretation.
transfer.explanation: The passage explicitly rejects universal generalization across all restorations and climates.
transfer.passage: Several restored wetlands in the region have attracted more bird species over five years. The report’s author welcomes the pattern but notes that rainfall also increased and that the sites were not selected randomly. The results are encouraging evidence about these projects. They do not establish that every restoration, in every climate, will produce the same outcome.
